strategies.name: Maize–Soybean–Maize Rotation
strategies.rationale: Inserting a legume (soybean) after a summer maize crop provides biological nitrogen fixation, reducing the need for synthetic nitrogen fertilizers. The legume’s root system improves soil structure and increases organic matter, while its residue enhances water infiltration for the following maize season.
expected_benefits: Improved soil fertility and nitrogen status
Higher soil organic matter and water‑holding capacity
risks_and_uncertainties: Soybean may not be fully adapted to the local temperature and rainfall pattern; yield could be lower than expected.
Soybean requires adequate winter irrigation; surface irrigation may be less efficient for a shallow crop.
Pest and disease pressure (e.g., soybean cyst nematode) could affect crop performance.
Market price for soybean may fluctuate, impacting profitability.
evidence_used: Crop Rotation An Approach To Secure Future Food by Samiha Ouda, Abd El-Hafeez Zohry, Tahany Noreldin
Assessing crop rotation as a climate-smart agriculture ...
Utilizing Different Crop Rotation Systems for Agricultural and Environmental Sustainability: A Review

strategies.name: Maize–Cover Crop–Maize Rotation
strategies.rationale: A winter cover crop provides continuous ground cover, suppresses weeds, and its residues decompose to build soil organic matter. This improves soil structure, reduces erosion, and enhances moisture retention for the subsequent maize crop.
expected_benefits: Increased soil organic matter and microbial activity
Improved water infiltration and reduced runoff
Reduced need for tillage and associated labor
risks_and_uncertainties: Cover crops may compete for water during the early growing season of the next maize crop, especially under surface irrigation.
Management of cover crop termination (timing, method) is critical; improper termination could reduce maize yield.
Cover crop establishment may be affected by winter rainfall variability; low precipitation could limit growth.
Economic return from cover crops is indirect; farmer must weigh labor and potential loss of cash crop area.
evidence_used: Crop Rotation: A Sustainable Practice for Soil and Water Conservation - Agriculture Notes by Agriculture.Institute
Utilizing Different Crop Rotation Systems for Agricultural and Environmental Sustainability: A Review

strategies.name: Maize–Winter Wheat–Maize Rotation
strategies.rationale: Winter wheat occupies the cooler, wetter part of the year, reducing competition for summer water resources. Wheat’s deep root system improves soil structure and can help break up compacted layers, while its residue contributes to organic matter buildup for the next maize season.
expected_benefits: Maintained crop productivity with a different grain crop
Improved soil structure and organic matter from wheat residue
risks_and_uncertainties: Winter wheat yield may be lower than maize, affecting overall profitability.
The crop may require additional irrigation during dry spells; surface irrigation may be less efficient.
Pest and disease pressures differ between wheat and maize; management plans must be adapted.
Market demand for wheat versus maize must be verified locally.
evidence_used: Crop Rotation An Approach To Secure Future Food by Samiha Ouda, Abd El-Hafeez Zohry, Tahany Noreldin

overall_notes: All strategies are based on general literature and climate data for the region; they are not site‑specific trials.
The NASA POWER data provide average temperature and precipitation but do not capture micro‑climate or soil moisture dynamics; actual irrigation scheduling should be verified locally.
Crop suitability (e.g., soybean, vetch, wheat) for the specific sandy loam, pH 7.5, and irrigation method (surface) has not been tested on Demo Farm; local agronomist input is required.
Market demand and price volatility for legumes or cover crops were not considered; economic feasibility should be assessed.
Water savings are qualitative; actual water use will depend on crop water requirements, irrigation efficiency, and rainfall during the growing season.
All strategies assume that the farmer can maintain the same irrigation frequency (every 10 days) and that the Nile canal supply is sufficient for the proposed rotations.
